# Why Izanagi belongs in the scholarly record

A name can be complete without carrying a ​single diacritic. **Izanagi** is a canonical scholarly spelling, not a damaged form waiting for decoration. This post follows the evidence behind that spelling: the Japanese characters record, the reconstructed sound, the myths, ‌the material culture, and the reasons this particular romanization became the public reference. The plain ASCII letters already contain the whole form. The scholarly work is to prove their provenance, preserve their ‌capitalization, and keep the name attached to its history.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Izanagi
- **ASCII form:** izanagi
- **Meaning:** "He who invites"
- **Domain of influence:** Creator God, Shintō
- **Pantheon:** Japanese
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent ​form
- **Original script:** 伊邪那岐 (Japanese characters)

## Overview

**Izanagi** (*izanagi*) — Creator God, Shintō · He who invites — belongs to the Japanese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Creator God, ​Shintō". The name means "He who invites".

**Izanagi** is the male half of the primordial creator pair. With his sister-wife Izanami he stirred the world-ocean with the jeweled spear and raised the ​islands of Japan; his failed rescue of her from Yomi founded the boundary of death; and his river purification afterward gave birth to the three rulers of heaven, night, and sea — ​including Amaterasu herself.

PuniCodex records the canonical scholarly spelling **Izanagi** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/izanagi/). The displayed form is ASCII-equivalent — a description computed from the displayed form itself. The ​plain ASCII form *izanagi* contains the same letters: no recovered diacritics or special encoding is claimed. The work here is consistent citation, capitalization, provenance, and cultural context.

## The Name

The name is ‌attested in Japanese characters as **伊邪那岐**. Etymologically it means "He who invites".

The canonical spelling **Izanagi** matches the conventional scholarly romanization. The plain ASCII form *izanagi* contains the same letters, so ​no lost diacritics or encoding transition is claimed. The editorial work is to fix one reviewed reference spelling, preserve capitalization and provenance, and keep the original evidence visible. The displayed form is ​ASCII-equivalent — a description computed from the displayed form itself.

## The Original Script

The name is written in Japanese characters as **伊邪那岐**. That attested script ​remains the primary evidence for the conventional romanization **Izanagi**. The canonical Latin spelling does not pretend to recover marks it never contained: it fixes one reviewed reference form while leaving the original ‌script visible for comparison.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/i.za.na.ɡi/** — Modern Standard Japanese (Hepburn).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **I-** — Close front [i]
- **-za-** — Voiced alveolar fricative [z] ​plus open central [a]
- **-na-** — Alveolar nasal [n] plus open central [a]
- **-gi** — Voiced velar stop [ɡ] plus close front [i]; from 岐 'invite'

For the modern speaker, the closest ‌approximation is: 'EE-zah-nah-gee' — the 'g' is hard, and the 'r' of Western transcriptions is absent in Japanese.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Japanese** — 伊邪那岐 (Izanagi), 'He-Who-Invites,' creator kami
- ​**Consort** — Izanami, 'She-Who-Invites'
- **Children** — Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi, Susanoo, and the kami of the islands, rivers, winds, and forges

Izanagi keeps its restoration plain: plain Hepburn. He is one of the two ​primordial creator kami of Japanese myth.

## Mythology

Izanagi's mythology is the creation narrative of the *Kojiki* and *Nihon Shoki*: the making of the land, the founding of death, and the birth ​of the gods who rule heaven and earth. It is also the story of a husband who **could not bring his wife back** — and of what he made instead.

### The Spear ​in the Brine (The Stirring)

When heaven and earth had parted but the land below floated like oil and drifted like a jellyfish, the heavenly kami commanded **Izanagi** and **Izanami** to make ​it solid. Standing upon the Floating Bridge of Heaven, they lowered the jeweled spear **Ame-no-Nuboko** and stirred; when they drew it up, brine dripped from the tip and piled up, congealing into ‌the island of Onogoroshima (Kojiki 1). Descending, they built a heavenly pillar and a hall eight fathoms long and prepared to beget the land. The image is the Japanese creation at its ​most elegant: the cosmos is not spoken or fought into being but stirred — order precipitating out of the world-ocean like salt from brine. Everything that follows, from the imperial line to ‌the boundary of death, crystallizes from that single drip.

### The Ceremony Spoken Ajar (The Wrong Word)

To seal their union, Izanagi and Izanami were to circle the heavenly pillar, he from the ​left and she from the right, meeting on the far side. But Izanami spoke first in greeting — a breach of ritual order — and though they coupled, their first child was ‌**Hiruko**, the leech-child, boneless and adrift, whom they set loose in a reed boat (Kojiki 1). Consulting the heavenly kami, they learned the error: the man's voice must come first. They ​redid the circuit in the correct order, and Izanami bore the eight great islands of Japan. The myth encodes a whole ritual theory — words spoken out of sequence pollute outcomes — ‌and plants cosmic law inside the smallest unit of ceremony: who speaks first at the pillar. No other creation story makes grammar itself a generative force.

### The Pursuit Beyond the Slope (Yomi)

​Giving birth to the fire god **Kagutsuchi**, Izanami was burned so badly that she died. Grieving, Izanagi followed her to Yomi and found her at the castle-hall, where she warned him not ‌to look until she had consulted the gods of that land. He waited — but broke his promise, lit a tooth of his comb, and saw his beloved rotting, maggot-crowned, with eight ​thunder-kami raging on her body. Horror-struck, he fled; the hags of Yomi and the thunders pursued him to the slope **Yomotsu-hirasaka**, where he hurled peaches at the pursuers and finally rolled a ​great boulder into the pass, crying: henceforth let no living cross to the dead (Kojiki 1). Behind the stone, Izanami pronounced the curse of daily death. The myth does not flinch: grief ‌violates the boundary it cannot abolish, and from that violation the world gains both its funerals and its peaches.

### The Slaying of the Fire Child (The Beheading)

Blaming Kagutsuchi for his wife's ‌death, Izanagi drew his ten-hand blade and cut the fire god's neck. From the blood on the blade's tip leaped the sword-gods Iwasaku and Nesaku; from the blood falling on the boulders ‌leaped the mountain-smith deities **Kanayamahiko and Kanayamahime**, patrons of metal and stone (Kojiki 1). He then committed Izanami's corpse to the mountains — the chronicle names her burial place as Mount ​Hiba in the land of Kibi — and, weeping, uttered the chronicle's first poem of mourning, from which later scholars read the very word kami as 'that which withdraws.' Even in vengeance ​the creation does not pause: every drop of the fire child's blood becomes a power of the forge. The myth binds grief to technology — the volcano that kills is the mountain ‌that yields ore.

### The Bath That Made the Gods (The Purification)

Returning from Yomi polluted, Izanagi purified himself at the river-mouth of Tachibana in Hyūga, casting off his accessories one by one ​— each became a kami, twelve in all, the patrons of ritual purification. Washing his left eye he begot **Amaterasu**, his right eye **Tsukuyomi**, his nose **Susanoo** (Kojiki 1). Then Izanagi, his ​work complete, 'dwelt at the palace of Taga,' and the chronicle adds that some say he departed at last to the land of the dead. The misogi he performed stands at the ‌head of every Shinto ablution to this day. The creation ends not with a throne but with a bath: the maker of the world must wash off the world before he can ​rest — purity, not power, is the final gift of the creator.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Izanagi concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement ​about the name:

- **Ame-no-Nuboko** — The jeweled spear given by the heavenly kami; the drip of brine from its tip congealed into Onogoroshima, the first island
- **Yomotsu-hirasaka** — The even slope of ‌Yomi's boundary, sealed by the great boulder — the frontier between the living and the dead
- **Misogi purification** — The river ritual that cleansed Yomi's pollution and generated the three sovereign ​kami; the ancestor of every Shinto ablution
- **The comb** — Izanagi's comb, whose lit tooth revealed Izanami's decay — knowledge that cannot be unlit
- **Peaches** — The fruits he hurled at Yomi's ‌pursuing hags, from which peaches took their power against evil in Japanese folk ritual

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material trail of the creation pair runs through shrine geography rather than monuments. Awaji ​Island — identified with Onogoroshima in local tradition — keeps their legend at Izanagi Jingū. Taga Taisha in Shiga Prefecture claims the site of Izanagi's retirement palace and preserves the medieval Taga-dera ​engi recounting the creation. The Kojiki's note that Izanami was buried on Mount Hiba links the myth to the Chūgoku region's ritual landscape. Shrine treasures and picture scrolls across Japan illustrate the ​spear-stirring and the Yomi pursuit, while the misogi rite itself — documented in the Engishiki's ritual protocols — remains a living layer of the tradition, performed daily at river-mouths and shrines.

## Realm ​& Domain

**Izanagi** is the male half of the primordial creator pair. With his sister-wife Izanami he stirred the world-ocean with the jeweled spear and raised the islands of Japan; his failed ‌rescue of her from Yomi founded the boundary of death; and his river purification afterward gave birth to the three rulers of heaven, night, and sea — including Amaterasu herself.

### Creator of ‌Japan

With Izanami, he stirred the ocean with the jeweled spear and raised the eight great islands.

### Spear of Heaven

Ame-no-Nuboko, the jeweled spear; the brine dripping from its tip became the ​first island.

### Father of the Sun

His misogi bath produced Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi, and Susanoo.

### Visitor to Yomi

He descended to the underworld to retrieve Izanami and sealed its door behind him.

## ‌Across Cultures

Izanagi and Izanami were drawn into Buddhist cosmology as the Japanese counterpart of cosmic parentage: in Ryōbu Shinto, Izanagi's stirring of the brine was read alongside the primal vibrations of ​Dainichi's two mandalas, and medieval Tendai assigned the pair places in its systems of correspondence between kami and buddhas. In the Meiji period, State Shinto elevated their creation narrative into national history, ​taught in school primers as the literal origin of the islands and the imperial line; after 1945 the myth returned to the status of myth, though the textbooks' version still shapes popular ‌understanding. Abroad, the couple stirring the primordial ocean has become one of the most recognizable images of Japanese mythology.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[amaterasu|Amaterasu]] (father and sun goddess), ‌[[izanami|Izanami]] (creation couple / Yomi separation), [[ahuramazda|AhuraMazdā]] (creator / cosmogonic), [[audhumla|Auðhumla]] (creator / cosmogonic), [[baiame|Baiame]] (creator / cosmogonic), and [[bunjil|Bunjil]] (creator / cosmogonic).

## Cultural Legacy

Misogi and its descendants — shrine ablutions, ‌sumo ring-purifications, and the cleansing rites of martial lineages — descend from Izanagi's bath. The creation couple crowns the genealogies recited at shrine festivals, and Onogoroshima tradition ties them to Awaji, whose ‌Izanagi Jingū preserves their legend. Every telling of the cave myth, every enthronement rite, every New-Year first-shrine visit quietly presupposes his cosmology: a world stirred from brine, lost to death, and washed ​back into light. Modern manga and games retell his descent to Yomi as readily as the Greeks retell Orpheus.

## The Scholarly Record

The account of Izanagi given in this edition rests on ‌the witnesses and reference works listed below. Lexica and etymological dictionaries secure the form and meaning of the name; the literary and religious texts supply the narrative evidence.

-  Nihon Shoki 1 (parallel creation accounts).
-  Philippi, Kojiki.
-  Aston, Nihongi.

## A Meditation

Izanagi's story is the biography of every maker: to create is to lose what you love ​to your own creation — his wife dies of the fire child, and the fire is also his child. His flight from Yomi gives Japan its boundary between life and death, and ​his bath gives it the idea that the sacred is what has been washed.

The myth refuses consolations: he cannot rescue Izanami, cannot unsee what he saw, cannot re-enter the cave. What ‌he can do is wash, and name, and give the world its ruling gods. In that modest sequence — grief, boundary, ablution, retirement — the Kojiki quietly describes how a person survives ​an unbearable loss: not by undoing it, but by cleansing the day that comes after.

The plain ASCII form *izanagi* ​contains the same letters, so there are no lost diacritics to recover and no special encoding transition to explain. The value here is not added decoration; it is fidelity to the attested record.

A canonical name is a small map. In the case of **Izanagi**, the route ​does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the conventional scholarly spelling already uses the Latin alphabet. The original evidence — **伊邪那岐** in Japanese characters — carries semantic and phonetic information ​that no romanization can fully reproduce.

By fixing one reviewed spelling as the public reference, the project prevents the drift that occurs when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, ‌and database. The character list shows exactly what is carried forward. "No change" here means a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and faithful to the record.
